result.summary: 2012 was nearly silent for Legg in public: his blog's only 2012 post was about Neil Armstrong, and his famous forecasts (AGI mean 2028, proto-AGI within 8 years) were posted on 31 Dec 2011. The one 2012 item is a borderline comment dated 8 January 2012 (the date comes from a search snippet) that restates the 8-year proto-AGI expectation. If that comment is ruled out, this is effectively a quiet year.

reply_text:
I found one weak candidate for 2012 and no strong one. Legg's main dated forecast from that period, an "impressive proto-AGI within the next 8 years" alongside human-level AGI with a mean of 2028, was posted on 31 December 2011. That makes it a 2011 claim, not a 2012 one.

- **The candidate:** an 8 January 2012 comment Legg wrote under that blog post, answering a reader. It mentions "the next 8 years" and "an impressive proto-AGI", but it is mainly about computer power, not a new forecast. It's borderline, so check it before counting it.
- **Its date is not confirmed by the page I opened.** The comment text I quote comes from the blog page. But the fetched text dropped the comment timestamps; I only saw "8 January, 2012 at 1:20 am" in search result snippets. The printed comment also looks cut off: the second sentence starts "Seeing the same again", with nothing before it saying what "the same" is. Check both on the live page.
- **Other comments with unknown dates:** in other replies on the same post, Legg describes an "acid test" for the proto-AGI and says this "might be my last annual prediction". The fetched text showed no dates for these, so I couldn't place them in 2011 or 2012 and left them out.
- **The rest of 2012 looks quiet.** His blog's only 2012 post (28 August) is about Neil Armstrong. I found no 2012 talk or interview carrying a timeline. An undated interview by Jonathan Despres on a fan wiki has timeline claims ("mid 2020's", "2025 to 2040"), but nothing ties it to 2012. Later write-ups citing "2011/2012" all point back to the December 2011 post.

I used 9 of 12 searches and 4 of 6 page openings. The first search's results were saved and shown again in the second step, not run twice.
